text: You get an integer array nums and an integer k. Return true if you can split the array into k non-empty subsets, and all of them have the same sum.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — every number is used exactly once, and it goes into exactly one subset. So each subset must sum to total divided by k. Is that right?
Got it. Are there any constraints on the input size?
k is at least one and at most the array length, which is at most sixteen. Each value is between one and ten to the fourth, and each value shows up at most four times.

OK. Only sixteen numbers, so an exponential search is fine. All values are positive, so non-empty comes for free: each subset needs a target of at least one. And the max total is sixteen times ten to the fourth, a hundred sixty thousand, so overflow is not a worry. Let me run through the examples. Four, three, two, three, five, two, one with k equals four: the sum is twenty, so each subset is five — five, one plus four, two plus three, two plus three. So true. One, two, three, four with k equals three: the sum is ten, and ten doesn't divide by three. So false right away.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to try all k to the n assignments and check the sums at the end. This problem reminds me of a bucket-filling backtracking search with symmetry pruning. Each number picks one of k buckets, so I build the assignment one number at a time and prune early: never let a bucket go over the target. There's also a second view — fill bucket one to the target, then bucket two, and so on. I'll start with the bucket view, because the pruning is simple and the code is short.

Here's the plan. One: if the total doesn't divide by k, return false; otherwise the target is total over k, and I sort descending. Two: each number tries the k buckets — skip one that would go over the target, or one with the same sum as its left neighbor, since that's the same state with buckets swapped. Three: place, recurse, undo; once every number is placed, return true. That's enough: the buckets add up to k times target and none is over, so each is exactly the target. One thing worth flagging — the sort is descending. Big numbers have the fewest places to go, so if they can't fit, I find out near the top of the tree. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. It's the plan almost line for line: sort, divisibility check, then exist places one number per level with the two skips, recursing and taking the number back. One thing worth flagging — both skip lines must be continue, not break. The buckets are not sorted, so a full bucket can come before an empty one. Take one, one with k equals two: the second one overflows bucket zero, and a break never tries the empty bucket one. So it returns false, but the answer is true. A break on the duplicate line is wrong too, just harder to catch: the smallest failing input has nine numbers.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Example one sorted is five, four, three, three, two, two, one, target five, expected true. The descending sort does the work: the five and four take their own buckets, and the small numbers fill the gaps. The row that matters is the last: the one overflows bucket zero and tops off the four, so every bucket is five. Eight calls, no undo — true. Example two is false with zero calls, since ten mod three isn't zero. Let's also test with corner cases. k equals one: always true. k equals n: true only if all values are equal. Odd total with k equals two: false, zero calls. Two, two, two, two, three, four, five with k equals four: the total divides, but it's false after twelve calls.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is k to the n in the worst case — each number has up to k choices. In practice the pruning is huge: the worst input I found took about two hundred seven thousand calls, around two milliseconds. The space complexity is O of n for the recursion stack, plus k buckets. Overflow: the worst total is a hundred sixty thousand, far below int max. And the total mod k check is just a shortcut. If I drop it, target rounds down, so k times target is less than the total. The numbers can never all fit, and the search still returns false. It's only slower.
How much do the sort and the duplicate check actually buy you?

I measured it on hard false cases with sixteen numbers: one with k equals four, and one with k equals eight and small values. The duplicate line is the big win. On the k equals eight case it's eight hundred forty-five calls with it, and over forty-one million without it — about six hundred five milliseconds instead of zero point zero one seven. With k equals eight, many buckets are equal, so there's a lot of symmetry to cut. On the k equals four case, dropping it goes from about two hundred seven thousand calls to almost five million. The descending sort is the second lever: ascending needs about three hundred fifty-four thousand calls on the k equals eight case. All variants are still correct; only the speed changes.
You mentioned the subset view. Is that ever better?

Yes, sometimes. The fill-one-bucket-at-a-time version keeps a used array. It fills one subset to the target, then starts the next one, and it's also correct. On the hard cases with k from three to five it makes far fewer calls: on the k equals four case, about seventeen hundred versus two hundred seven thousand. But on the k equals eight case it's about a hundred twenty-seven thousand versus eight hundred forty-five. So neither one wins every time. If I want a guaranteed bound, I'd use a bitmask DP over the set of used numbers, storing the sum of the subset I'm filling. Taking that sum mod target means a full subset resets to zero, and the next number starts a new one. That's n times two to the n time and two to the n space — sixty-five thousand five hundred thirty-six states, a few milliseconds at most.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You framed it as a k-bucket search and pruned it from the start. You explained why both skip lines are continue, not break, with a concrete counterexample. And you backed the duplicate check with numbers — eight hundred forty-five versus over forty-one million calls — then showed the trade-off against the fill-one-bucket version. Good work.
